Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

The thermodynamics of nucleic acid processes is heavily affected by the electric double-layer of micro-ions around the polyions. We focus here on the Coulombic contribution to the salt-polyelectrolyte preferential interaction (Donnan) coefficient and we report extremely accurate analytical expressions valid in the range of low salt concentration (when polyion radius is smaller than the Debye length). The analysis is performed at Poisson-Boltzmann level, in cylindrical geometry, with emphasis on highly charged poly-ions (beyond ``counter-ion condensation''). The results hold for any electrolyte of the form $z_-$:$z_+$. We also obtain a remarkably accurate expression for the electric potential in the vicinity of the poly-ion.

The thermodynamics of nucleic acid processes is strongly shaped by the electric double layer formed by mobile micro-ions around charged macromolecules, or polyions. In systems such as DNA and RNA, this ionic atmosphere affects key physical and biochemical phenomena, including folding, hybridization, ligand binding, and conformational transitions. Because nucleic acids are highly charged polyelectrolytes, their interaction with surrounding salt ions must be described carefully in order to understand their stability and thermodynamic behavior in solution.

The central focus of the analysis is the Coulombic contribution to the salt–polyelectrolyte preferential interaction, also known as the Donnan coefficient. This quantity measures how the presence of a charged polyion perturbs the local distribution of salt ions relative to the bulk solution. In other words, it characterizes the excess or depletion of ions caused by electrostatic interactions between the polyion and the surrounding electrolyte. Such preferential interactions are important because they directly contribute to the salt dependence of thermodynamic observables.

The work provides highly accurate analytical expressions for the Donnan coefficient in the low-salt regime. This regime is defined by the condition that the radius of the polyion is smaller than the Debye screening length, meaning that electrostatic interactions extend over distances larger than the physical size of the charged cylinder. Under these conditions, the ionic atmosphere is diffuse, and the electrostatic potential varies over a relatively long range. Analytical results in this limit are especially valuable because they offer simple yet precise descriptions of complex ion distributions without requiring full numerical solutions.

The theoretical treatment is based on the Poisson–Boltzmann framework applied in cylindrical geometry, which is appropriate for rod-like polyelectrolytes such as nucleic acids. The analysis emphasizes the case of highly charged polyions, particularly beyond the classical counter-ion condensation threshold. In this regime, the polyion charge is large enough that counter-ions accumulate strongly near its surface, partially neutralizing the bare charge and producing nonlinear electrostatic effects. Capturing these effects requires going beyond simple linearized Debye–Hückel theory.

The results are general and apply to electrolytes of arbitrary valence asymmetry of the form \(z_-:z_+\), where \(z_-\) and \(z_+\) denote the valences of the co-ions and counter-ions, respectively. In addition to expressions for the preferential interaction coefficient, the analysis yields an accurate formula for the electric potential near the polyion. This near-field potential is essential for describing the structure of the ionic atmosphere close to the charged macromolecule and provides a foundation for understanding salt effects in a broad range of nucleic acid and polyelectrolyte systems.

Electric double layers play a central role in determining the thermodynamic behavior of nucleic acids and other highly charged polyelectrolytes in electrolyte solutions. Because nucleic acids carry a large negative charge density along their backbone, they strongly perturb the surrounding distribution of mobile ions. This redistribution of counterions and coions affects the free energy of the system and therefore influences salt-dependent processes such as duplex formation, folding, condensation, and ligand binding. A useful way to quantify these effects is through the salt-polyelectrolyte preferential interaction coefficient, which measures how the presence of the polyelectrolyte changes the local abundance of salt relative to the bulk solution.

The text analyzes the Coulombic contribution to this preferential interaction coefficient using Poisson-Boltzmann theory. In this framework, the polyelectrolyte is modeled as a charged cylinder surrounded by an electrolyte solution, and the electrostatic potential is obtained by solving the nonlinear Poisson-Boltzmann equation in cylindrical geometry. Particular attention is given to the low-salt regime, where the electric double layer extends far from the polyion and where analytical descriptions are especially valuable. This regime is highly relevant for nucleic acids because their large charge density produces strong electrostatic fields and substantial counterion accumulation near the molecular surface.

A major focus of the analysis is the derivation of accurate analytical expressions for highly charged polyions in general electrolyte solutions. Rather than relying only on limiting laws or approximate numerical treatments, the work develops formulas that capture the behavior of the electrostatic potential and the associated ion distributions with high precision. These expressions are applicable to a broad class of electrolytes, including asymmetric salts, and therefore extend beyond the simplest case of monovalent counterions and coions.

An important result is a precise analytical description of the electric potential in the near-polyion region. This near-field potential is crucial because much of the excess counterion accumulation and coion exclusion occurs close to the charged cylinder. Small inaccuracies in this region can lead to significant errors in calculated thermodynamic quantities. By improving the representation of the near-polyion potential, the analysis provides a more reliable basis for evaluating the Coulombic component of preferential interactions.

The derived expressions clarify how the electrostatic properties of the double layer depend on polyion charge density, ion valence, salt concentration, and cylindrical geometry. They also show how the nonlinear character of the Poisson-Boltzmann equation governs ion condensation and the salt dependence of polyelectrolyte thermodynamics. For highly charged systems such as DNA and RNA, these effects cannot be adequately described by simple linearized theories, making the nonlinear analytical treatment especially important.

Overall, the text provides a refined theoretical framework for understanding salt effects in nucleic acid and polyelectrolyte systems. By combining cylindrical Poisson-Boltzmann theory with highly accurate low-salt analytical solutions, it significantly improves quantitative predictions of preferential interaction coefficients and related thermodynamic properties. These results offer a stronger foundation for interpreting experiments on nucleic acid stability, folding, and association in electrolyte solutions, and they contribute to the broader theoretical description of charged macromolecules in ionic environments.

**The Coulombic Donnan Effect**

The Coulombic Donnan effect describes how charged particles distribute themselves across a semipermeable membrane when some ions cannot freely pass through it. This situation often occurs in biological systems, gels, membranes, and colloidal materials.

In a Donnan equilibrium, mobile ions move across a membrane in response to concentration differences. However, if one side contains fixed charged groups—such as proteins, polyelectrolytes, or charged polymer networks—these immobile charges create an electrical imbalance. Coulombic interactions, meaning the attractive and repulsive forces between charged particles, then influence how ions arrange themselves.

For example, if a gel contains fixed negative charges, positive ions are attracted into the gel, while negative ions are partially excluded. As a result, the ion concentrations inside and outside the gel become unequal. This difference can create an electrical potential known as the Donnan potential, as well as osmotic pressure that may cause the gel to swell.

The Coulombic Donnan effect is important in many fields. In biology, it helps explain ion balance in cells and tissues. In chemistry and materials science, it is used to understand membranes, hydrogels, water purification systems, and ion-exchange materials. Overall, the effect shows how electrostatic forces and membrane permeability work together to control the distribution of ions in charged environments.

Treating the nucleic acid as a uniformly charged cylinder embedded in a continuum electrolyte, we derive ion distributions, electrostatic potentials, and salt-dependent screening behavior beyond the linearized approximation. The theory highlights the role of counterion condensation, cylindrical geometry, and nonlinear electrostatics in controlling the spatial organization of mobile ions near DNA- or RNA-like polyelectrolytes. At low bulk salt concentration, the electrostatic environment is governed by a competition between condensed counterions and diffuse salt ions, producing characteristic deviations from Debye–Hückel screening. These results provide a framework for interpreting salt-dependent stability, interactions, and conformational behavior of highly charged nucleic acids in dilute electrolyte solutions.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a journal-style summary describing research on the Coulombic contribution to the Donnan coefficient for nucleic acid polyions in asymmetric electrolytes using cylindrical Poisson-Boltzmann theory.
counterfactuals.output:
**Journal-style summary**

The Coulombic contribution to the Donnan coefficient of nucleic acid polyions was examined within the framework of cylindrical Poisson–Boltzmann (PB) theory, with emphasis on asymmetric supporting electrolytes. Nucleic acids such as DNA and RNA were modeled as uniformly charged, impenetrable cylinders surrounded by a concentric cylindrical cell containing mobile ions. The electrostatic potential was obtained from the nonlinear PB equation subject to boundary conditions of fixed polyion charge density at the molecular surface and electroneutrality at the cell boundary. This treatment permits evaluation of the excess ionic distributions generated by the polyion field and their contribution to Donnan partitioning between the polyelectrolyte phase and an external salt reservoir.

Particular attention was given to electrolytes with unequal counterion and coion valences, since ion-valence asymmetry strongly modifies both counterion accumulation and coion exclusion near highly charged nucleic acid surfaces. The analysis shows that the Coulombic part of the Donnan coefficient is controlled by the nonlinear screening cloud surrounding the polyion rather than by bulk electroneutrality alone. Multivalent counterions are predicted to reduce the magnitude of the electrostatic potential more efficiently than monovalent ions, leading to a smaller Donnan imbalance at comparable ionic strength. Conversely, multivalent coions enhance exclusion effects and can increase the Coulombic contribution to the Donnan coefficient.

The cylindrical PB calculations demonstrate that the Donnan coefficient depends sensitively on nucleic acid charge density, polyion concentration, salt concentration, and electrolyte valence composition. At low salt, counterion condensation-like behavior emerges naturally from the nonlinear PB solution, producing a saturation in the effective electrostatic contribution. At higher salt, screening suppresses the long-range potential, and the Coulombic Donnan term decreases toward the weak-coupling limit. The effect is more pronounced for DNA-like charge densities, where the high linear charge density produces strong ion redistribution even at moderate salt concentrations.

Overall, the study establishes cylindrical PB theory as a useful continuum framework for separating the Coulombic contribution to Donnan equilibria from nonelectrostatic effects such as ion-specific binding, hydration, and excluded volume. The results indicate that electrolyte asymmetry must be explicitly included when interpreting Donnan measurements on nucleic acid solutions, gels, or dense phases, particularly in the presence of divalent or multivalent ions. While the mean-field PB approach neglects ion–ion correlations and molecular details, it provides a tractable baseline for understanding how electrostatics governs ion partitioning around cylindrical nucleic acid polyions.

counterfactuals.prompt: Please draft an academic abstract about electric double-layer effects on nucleic acid thermodynamics, focusing on low-salt analytical expressions for preferential interaction coefficients beyond counter-ion condensation.
counterfactuals.output:
**Abstract**

Electrostatic interactions are central to nucleic acid stability, yet their thermodynamic signatures at low salt remain difficult to describe using counter-ion condensation alone. Here we develop an analytical framework for electric double-layer contributions to nucleic acid thermodynamics in the dilute-salt regime, with emphasis on preferential interaction coefficients that quantify ion and water redistribution upon conformational or hybridization transitions. Starting from a continuum electrostatic description of a charged cylindrical polyelectrolyte, we derive low-salt expressions for salt-dependent excess chemical potentials and the corresponding preferential interaction coefficients, retaining finite double-layer structure rather than invoking a fully condensed counter-ion population. The resulting formulas separate contributions from local charge neutralization, diffuse ionic atmosphere relaxation, and changes in electrostatic self-energy, thereby clarifying the origin of logarithmic and sub-logarithmic salt dependences commonly observed in nucleic acid folding and duplex formation. Unlike standard condensation-based estimates, the expressions explicitly account for the sensitivity of ion uptake or release to molecular radius, charge density, dielectric environment, and transition-induced changes in electrostatic boundary conditions. This approach predicts that preferential interaction coefficients need not be constant even in experimentally accessible low-salt limits, and that deviations from ideal counter-ion release can arise from diffuse-layer expansion, co-ion exclusion, and incomplete electrostatic screening. The theory provides compact analytical relations connecting measured salt derivatives of melting temperatures, binding free energies, and folding equilibria to microscopic double-layer properties. These results offer a route to interpreting low-ionic-strength nucleic acid thermodynamics beyond the counter-ion condensation paradigm and establish a basis for comparing continuum electrostatic, molecular simulation, and experimental measurements of ion–nucleic acid coupling.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize a paper that derives accurate analytical formulas for the electrostatic potential near highly charged polyelectrolytes of cylindrical geometry in general \(z_-\!:\!z_+\) electrolytes.
counterfactuals.output:
The paper develops accurate analytical expressions for the electrostatic potential around a highly charged cylindrical polyelectrolyte immersed in a general asymmetric electrolyte of valences \(z_-:z_+\). The problem is treated within nonlinear Poisson–Boltzmann theory, focusing especially on the near-field region close to the charged cylinder, where linear Debye–Hückel theory fails.

The main physical system is an infinitely long charged cylinder of radius \(a\), line charge density \(\lambda\), and Manning parameter

\[
\xi=\frac{\ell_B \lambda}{e},
\]

where \(\ell_B\) is the Bjerrum length. The surrounding electrolyte contains coions of valence \(z_-\) and counterions of valence \(z_+\), so the electrostatic potential obeys the cylindrical Poisson–Boltzmann equation appropriate to a \(z_-:z_+\) salt.

A central goal of the paper is to obtain simple but quantitatively accurate formulas for the reduced potential

\[
\phi(r)=\frac{e\psi(r)}{k_B T}
\]

near the cylinder, including the strongly nonlinear regime relevant for highly charged polyelectrolytes such as DNA.

The authors exploit known exact and asymptotic properties of the cylindrical Poisson–Boltzmann equation. In particular, they use the fact that in special cases the equation is related to Painlevé III transcendents, whose short-distance and large-distance expansions can be matched. This allows them to derive analytical relations between the bare charge, the near-field potential, and the far-field or effective charge.

For highly charged cylinders, the potential close to the surface exhibits a universal behavior associated with counterion condensation. The bare charge no longer controls the far-field potential directly; instead, the system is characterized by a saturated effective charge. The paper generalizes previous results, mostly known for symmetric \(1:1\) electrolytes, to arbitrary \(z_-:z_+\) salts.

A key outcome is a set of compact near-field formulas for \(\phi(r)\) in the limit of small \(\kappa r\), where \(\kappa^{-1}\) is the Debye screening length. These formulas capture both the logarithmic Coulombic behavior near the cylinder and the nonlinear corrections induced by the electrolyte. They are expressed in terms of the Manning parameter, the cylinder radius, the salt valences, and integration constants determined by matching to the far-field solution.

The paper also derives the critical Manning parameter for counterion condensation in asymmetric electrolytes. In general, condensation occurs when the electrostatic attraction of counterions to the cylinder exceeds thermal energy. The threshold depends on the counterion valence and takes the form

\[
z_+ \xi = 1,
\]

so multivalent counterions lower the bare line charge density required for condensation.

For \(\xi\) above this threshold, the near-field potential enters a condensed-counterion regime. The analytical solution then involves a renormalized or effective charge that saturates at large bare charge. The paper provides formulas for this saturated effective charge as a function of the salt asymmetry. These results are important because charge renormalization controls the large-distance interaction between polyelectrolytes.

The authors compare their analytical expressions with numerical solutions of the full nonlinear Poisson–Boltzmann equation and find excellent agreement over the parameter ranges relevant to highly charged cylindrical macromolecules. The formulas remain accurate even for strongly charged cylinders and asymmetric electrolytes, where simpler approximations are unreliable.

The work is especially relevant for DNA and other stiff polyelectrolytes in the presence of multivalent ions. It gives a practical analytical way to estimate the electrostatic potential near such molecules without solving the nonlinear Poisson–Boltzmann equation numerically.

In summary, the paper:

- studies nonlinear electrostatics near highly charged cylindrical polyelectrolytes;
- treats general asymmetric \(z_-:z_+\) electrolytes;
- derives accurate near-field analytical formulas for the electrostatic potential;
- generalizes Manning condensation and charge-renormalization results beyond \(1:1\) salts;
- connects near-field behavior to far-field effective charge using asymptotic matching;
- validates the formulas against numerical Poisson–Boltzmann solutions;
- provides useful expressions for systems such as DNA in monovalent or multivalent salt solutions.

The main significance is that it turns a difficult nonlinear cylindrical Poisson–Boltzmann problem into a set of usable analytical formulas that retain high accuracy even in the strongly charged regime.

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a technical abstract for a study of micro-ion distributions around charged nucleic acids, including Donnan salt-polyelectrolyte coefficients, Debye-length limits, and Poisson-Boltzmann theory.
counterfactuals.output:
**Abstract**

We present a theoretical and computational study of micro-ion distributions surrounding charged nucleic acids in electrolyte solution, with emphasis on the coupling between fixed polyelectrolyte charge, mobile counterions and co-ions, Donnan partitioning, and electrostatic screening. Nucleic acids are modeled as highly charged cylindrical or atomistically resolved polyelectrolytes immersed in monovalent and mixed-valence salt reservoirs. Ion profiles are analyzed using nonlinear Poisson–Boltzmann theory and compared with limiting Debye–Hückel behavior at large distances from the macromolecular surface. The framework yields local electrostatic potentials, radial ion-density distributions, charge-compensation fractions, and salt-exclusion effects as functions of bulk ionic strength, nucleic-acid charge density, molecular geometry, and boundary conditions.

A central objective is the evaluation of Donnan salt–polyelectrolyte coefficients that quantify the preferential accumulation of counterions and depletion of co-ions in the nucleic-acid domain relative to the external salt reservoir. These coefficients are derived from electroneutrality constraints and ion chemical-potential matching across the polyelectrolyte/solution interface, and are related to experimentally accessible osmotic and activity-coefficient measurements. In the dilute-polyelectrolyte limit, the results recover classical Debye-length scaling, in which the electrostatic potential decays over the screening length \(\kappa^{-1}\), while deviations emerge when the Debye length becomes comparable to the nucleic-acid radius, interhelical spacing, or cell-model boundary. At low salt concentration, nonlinear counterion condensation and Donnan exclusion dominate the micro-ion atmosphere; at high salt concentration, ion distributions approach the linearized Poisson–Boltzmann regime with reduced polyelectrolyte-specific partitioning.

The analysis demonstrates that Donnan coefficients provide a compact thermodynamic measure of the ion atmosphere, linking microscopic Poisson–Boltzmann ion profiles to macroscopic salt partitioning and osmotic pressure. The study clarifies the Debye-length limits of continuum electrostatics for nucleic acids and identifies regimes in which nonlinear screening, finite geometry, and reservoir coupling must be retained. These results provide a quantitative basis for interpreting ion-dependent stability, folding, hybridization, and intermolecular interactions of DNA and RNA in electrolyte environments.
